texts.facts: 4. The facts giving rise to this appeal are that on 31.01.2012 at about 7 pm, Food & Safety Officer, Sh. Suniti Kumar Gupta lifted a sample of 'Sweet Corn' from Sh. Vimal Kishore S/o Dr. Suresh Kumar, Domino Pizza (a Unit of M/s Jubilant Food Works Ltd), Saket PVR New Delhi17 for analysis under the Food Safety and Standard Act 2006 and Rules/Regulations made there under (hereinafter referred to as FSS Act). Efforts were made to get the public witness to join the sample proceedings but none came forward and on request, Ms. Usha Kiran, FSO joined as witness to the sample proceedings. The sample consisted of eight sealed tins each containing 8 x 285 grams of 'Sweet Corn' taken as such in original condition bearing identical label declaration. The sample was divided into four equal parts then and there by the FSO by converting one sealed tin of 'Sweet Corn' as one counter part of the sample. Each counterpart containing the sample was separately packed, fastened, sealed and the signatures of FBO were obtained on the D.O. slip and wrapper of the tins containing the sample as per the prescribed procedure. The panchnama in Form V A was prepared and the signature of Sh. Vimal Kishore (appellant no. 1), FBO was obtained as a token of its acknowledgment. A price of Rs. 400/ was paid to the appellant no. 1 vide Food Business Operator receipt dated 31.01.2012. Thereafter, one counter part of the aforesaid sample bearing Designated Officer's code number 08/DO04/1343 alongwith one copy of form VI in a sealed packet and another copy of memo in Form VI in a separate sealed cover were sent separately to Food Analyst, Delhi for analysis on 01.02.2012. The FBO did not request to send the fourth part of the sample for analysis from NABL, Accredited Laboratory under Rule 2.4.5 of the Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011. Another two counterparts of the sample in a sealed packet alongwith two copies of form VI as well as the fourth counterpart in a separate sealed packet alongwith one copy of form VI were deposited with Designated Officer Sh. K.K. Mittal on Sh. Vimal Kishore vs State on 15 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76262855/ 2 01.02.2012. The Food Analyst vide his report no. PFA/Enf./229/2012 dated 10.02.2012 has reported that "the sample is misbranded because there is violation of Regulation No. 2.2.2.10 of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labeling) Regulation, 2011. However the sample conform to standard". Consequently, a complaint was filed against six persons including the appellants herein before the Ld. ADM South, who after hearing all the parties enforced a penalty of Rs. 15,000/ each upon appellant no. 1 and 2 and Rs. 20,000/ on the respondent no. 6 M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. (therein) for violation of regulation no. 2.2.2.10 of the FSS Act (packages and labelling regulation). 5. behalf of which its representative has sold some articles
texts.arguments: 6. The main contention raised by the Ld. Counsel for the appellants is that the appellants had purchased the articles sweet corn from M/s. Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. in a sealed condition and sold further in the same condition against the proper bills/invoice bearing serial no. 2044 dated 21.11.2011 issued by M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. and the said supply to the appellant no. 2 was not disputed by M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. during the adjudication proceedings. Even the packets of the sweet corn were not tampered with in any manner. As per the Public Analyst Report, the sampled article was conformed to standard but the same was opined to be misbranded on account non mentioning of "Best Before date". He further argued that the appellants were neither the manufacturer nor the packer of the sampled commodity and thus, the defence of due diligence should have been extended to them and as such, the appellants were liable to be protected by the warranty of M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. as provided in Section the importer/supplier of the sampled article and appellant's role was limited to sale of the sealed packet in the same condition as purchased by them from M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. and as such, impugned order is not sustainable against them. To support his contentions, he has placed reliance upon the judgment P. Unnikrishnan Vs. Food Inspector, Palghat Municipally, Palghat, Kerala State, AIR 1995 SC 1983 wherein t h e i r l o r d s h i p s w e r e p l e a s e d t o h e l d t h a t C r i m i n a l - C o n v i c t i o n - S e c t i o n 1 9 ( 2 ) o f P r e v e n t i o n o f F o o d Adulteration Act - Magistrate had acquitted Accused who were tried for an offence under Section 7(1) read with Section 16(1A)(a)(i) of Act - High Court had reversed order o f a c q u i t t a l a n d c o n v i c t e d A p p e l l a n t - H e n c e , t h i s A p p e a l - . 7. Per contra, the Ld. Addl. PP has refuted the entire line of arguments whilst making submissions that the Food Safety Officer was within its power to lift the sample of Sweet Corn. Before proceeding further, let me quote the relevant statutory provision: Section 2 (ix) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 describes 'misbranding' of an article of food.
